newsitem.title: USA: Cholesterol key to embryo development - study.
newsitem.headline: Cholesterol key to embryo development - study.

text.p: Cholesterol, a notorious nutritional villain, got a boost on Wednesday from research that shows it is critical to embryonic development -- but that is not a cue to pile on the butter and eggs.

Cholesterol, found in such fatty foods as butter, cheese, red meat and eggs, acts as an "anchor" for a gene called Sonic Hedgehog which helps determine how embryonic fruit flies develop, according to an article in the journal Science.

The same Sonic Hedgehog gene exists in mammals, including humans, said Philip Beachy, who co-wrote one of two articles on the phenomenon. Cholesterol makes the genetic protein interact with cell membranes during embryo development, sending the proper signal to the cells so that they develop normally, Beachy said.

Without a cholesterol molecule, the gene fails in the essential area of embryonic patterning, he and other researchers said. Such a lack in laboratory experiments has produced a deformed specimen, with one cyclopic eye and a tube-like nose with a single nostril.

But even though cholesterol has a key role to play, there is no reason to ingest more of it, Beachy said in a telephone interview from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore.

"It's possible that diet could affect these things ... but humans can synthesize cholesterol. ... It doesn't necessarily make sense for mothers to go on a high-fat diet and in fact there are probably good reasons for them not to do so."

But people with a rare genetic condition called Smith-Lemli-Opitz Syndrome are unable to make their own cholesterol and the lack of it has been linked to birth defects ranging from mild to extreme, Beachy said.
Future research was expected to focus on whether cholesterol acts as an anchor or enabler to other genes besides the Sonic Hedgehog gene, he said.
Cholesterol has been villified by nutritionists and cardiologists as the artery-clogging agent that is a major factor in heart disease.

But self-indulgent diners may take heart in research published last month in British medical journal The Lancet: a scientist at the University of California-Davis found that two appealing substances -- chocolate and red wine -- play some part in keeping cholesterol from sticking to human arteries.
